extracted.intended_audience: students and coaches preparing for mathematical olympiads / contest problem solvers (number theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and evaluative principles for solving/constructing solutions to olympiad-style number theory and combinatorics problems (modular arguments, congruences, factorization, bounding, functional equations). Emphasizes which reductions, congruences, and constructions to try and how to rule out cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digit-sum congruence modulo 9
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of the digits of a number is congruent to the number modulo 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to restrict possible digit sums of perfect squares (they must be congruent to 0,1,4,7 mod 9). Construct explicit squares of the form (10^m − k)^2 to realize desired digit-sum residues; examples given for n = 9m, 9m+1, 9m+4, 9m−2 with explicit choices of k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use factorial divisibility to rule out residues
rubrics_metrics.description: High factorials are divisible by large powers of primes (e.g., for y>5, y! divisible by 9), so adding constants yields predictable residues modulo those primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply such divisibility to show expressions like y! + 2001 have a nonresidue modulo 9, thereby eliminating all sufficiently large y and reducing to a finite check of small y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digit-count bounds combined with modular congruences
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare number of digits and digit permutations to obtain inequalities; combine with congruences (e.g., mod 9) to derive contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If 2^m is a permutation of 2^n, show they must have same number of digits ⇒ 2^n < 10·2^m ⇒ n−m ≤ 3; then use congruence modulo 9 and coprimality to show impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound digit sums via digit-count and refine by congruence
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper-bound digit-sum by counting digits (maximizing digits gives max digit-sum) and then use congruence classes to pick the unique small candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: estimate number of digits < 20,000 ⇒ max digit-sum ≤45, further bound B ≤12, then use congruence mod 9 of the big number to determine the exact small value (7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce modulo prime and compare to quadratic residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce both sides modulo a chosen prime and compare possible residues with the set of quadratic residues to rule out equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mod 11 analysis of x^10 and x^5 residues shows RHS residues (6,7,8) not in quadratic residues {0,1,3,4,5,9} ⇒ no integer solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit multiplicative group structure modulo p to limit k-th powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the structure of (Z/pZ)^× (its order and subgroup sizes) to enumerate residues attainable by cubes, fourth powers, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: modulo 13 the cubes give {0,1,5,8,12} and fourth powers {0,1,3,9}; sum of such residues cannot produce 7 mod 13, so a given congruence is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete the square to reduce to Pell-type and then use modular obstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform equations by completing the square to Pell-type forms and then reduce modulo an appropriate prime to check impossibility via residue classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: multiply by 4, rewrite as (2x+3y)^2 − 17y^2 = 488, then reduce modulo 17 and compare residues to show 488 cannot be represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use congruences modulo prime powers and factorial divisibility for perfect-power tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine divisibility of factorials by prime powers and congruences modulo those prime powers to exclude perfect-power possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for sums of factorials, show sum ≡ 9 (mod 27) though any sum of a! for a ≥9 is divisible by 27, contradiction. For cubes, use modulo 49 residue arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find minimal digit-sum multiple by examining few nonzero digits and 10^k mod n
rubrics_metrics.description: When minimizing digit-sum among multiples of n, consider numbers with very few nonzero digits (1s) and compute powers of 10 modulo n to locate the smallest such number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for n=29 look for smallest 10^n + 1 divisible by 29; list powers of 10 mod 29 to find exponent 14 where 10^14 ≡ 28 so 10^14+1 divisible by 29.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Euler's theorem and iterated reduction of exponents via φ(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Euler's theorem a^{φ(n)} ≡ 1 (mod n) for gcd(a,n)=1 and reduce large exponents modulo φ(n), iterating reduction through successive φ-values when exponents themselves are huge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to compute 5^{5555} (mod 25) reduce exponent modulo φ(25)=20, then φ(20)=8, etc, repeatedly reducing to manageable size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use congruences modulo composites and auxiliary primes to narrow residue possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce unknowns modulo various moduli (including composite moduli or different primes) to obtain a small list of possible residues, then rule out remaining cases by further modular checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deduce possible n residues modulo 9, eliminate some via modulo 37 computations, leaving only n ≥ 11 then combine with other inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show coloring depends only on residue classes to deduce monochromatic sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that color of elements depends only on their residue modulo k and propagate equalities via sequences of residue-class mappings to conclude whole set monochromatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: define Ai sets of residues modulo k, show Ai and A−i same color, then propagate Ai → An−i → ... and use gcd(k,n)=1 to cover all classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze parity and use factorization in exponential Diophantine equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parity arguments and factor the expressions (often into factors differing by small amounts) to force each factor to be a pure power and derive contradictions or solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 3^x − 2^y = 1, parity forces x even; write 2^y = (2m+1)^2 − 1 = 4m(4m+1) and deduce impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small-modulus reductions (mod 2,4,8,3,5,7, etc.) to constrain exponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce equations modulo small bases to deduce parity or congruence constraints on exponents, dramatically limiting possible cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples throughout: mod 8 to limit residues of 3^x, mod 5 to determine possible squares, mod 3/7 to deduce parity or gcd relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a product equals a prime power, each factor must be a power of that prime
rubrics_metrics.description: If (y+1)(y^2−y+1) is a power of 3, then each factor must itself be a power of 3; use squaring/subtraction to relate exponents and solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deduce existence of α,β with y+1 = 3^α and y^2−y+1 = 3^β, square and subtract to find β and hence y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use binomial-coefficient divisibility and p-adic valuation to determine highest prime power dividing an expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand expressions via binomial theorem and note divisibility of binomial coefficients by p to find the exact power of p dividing the expression and deduce exponent relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in px = (pn − 1)^p + 1 expansion, show highest power dividing RHS is p^{n+1} leading to x = n + 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split close factors differing by small integers and analyze gcd constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When product factors differ by a small integer (like z+1 and z−1), use their relative gcd and prime-power structure to enumerate cases and eliminate most.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (z+1)(z−1) = 2^x 3^y; at most one factor divisible by 3 and exactly one divisible by 4, leading to small explicit cases to check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use known integer identities to guess solutions and then prove uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize classical triples or identities (e.g., Pythagorean triple (5,12,13)) as candidate solutions and then use modular and factorization arguments to show no others exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: identify x=y=2,z=13 from (5,12,13) then eliminate all other possibilities by congruence reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare magnitudes of sums of powers via binomial expansion to rule out large exponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Use binomial expansion of (a+1)^n or bounds on individual terms to compare sums and show inequalities impossible for large n, leaving only small n solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show 11^n + 6^n + 5^n > 11^n expansion implies only n = 2 or 4 can satisfy a given equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use growth comparisons of exponentials to derive contradictions (exponential dominance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare growth rates like z^z vs x^x to show inequalities impossible (e.g., zz > xx + yy), using that increasing the base/exponent increases value drastically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for xx + yy = zz, show zz ≥ 2xx leading to contradiction since zz > xx + yy for positive integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate exponentials using (1 + k/n)^n < e^k to compare signs and sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the inequality (1 + k/n)^n < e^k to bound exponential expressions and deduce whether xy − yx is positive or negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: study sign of xy − yx by writing as yy((1 + k/y)^y − yk) and applying the e^k bound to rule out large parameter ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use iterates / orbit analysis for functional equations to deduce injectivity and contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the map g(n) = f(f(n)) and orbits {n, g(n), g(g(n)), ...} to deduce injectivity, pairing of preimages, or parity issues that can rule out functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: f(f(n)) = n + 1987 forces pairing of 1..1987 under f; odd count leads to contradiction, so no such f exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage bijectivity/surjectivity with well-ordering to force function equality
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ≥ g pointwise and f is surjective while g is bijective, use the well-ordering principle (smallest counterexample) to show f = g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prove uniqueness of a bijective solution g(n)=n+(−1)^n by showing any surjective f ≥ g would miss a value, contradicting surjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove injectivity then use process-of-elimination induction for functional equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Show f is injective (often by comparing f(f(a)+...) values) to deduce f(1)=1 and then perform induction: if f(k)=k for k< n then f(n)=n by elimination of smaller outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: multiple problems where injectivity + surjectivity + minimal-element arguments force f(n)=n for all n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize the range as multiples of the minimal nonzero element and derive general form
rubrics_metrics.description: If range T of f contains a minimal positive element a, show T = {multiples of a} and derive explicit formula f(qa+r) = (nr + q)a for 0 ≤ r < a, classifying all solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in IMO 1996 problem, define a as smallest nonzero element of T and prove the described structure; then check these functions satisfy the equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct multiplicative bijections by mapping primes in specified congruence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: To build multiplicative bijections between sets of integers constrained by congruence forms (e.g., 3n+1 and 4n+1), construct a bijection h between primes of the corresponding residue classes and extend multiplicatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: map primes of the form 3n+1 and 3n+2 to primes of the form 4n+1 and 4n+3 respectively, then define g on products to get multiplicativity g(xy)=g(x)g(y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use monotonicity plus factorization to extend small verified values to all n
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove small initial values f(1..k) equal to identity; then use multiplicativity/relative primality (n and n−1 coprime) and monotonicity to extend f(n)=n for all n via induction and constructing sequences tending to ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show f(3)=3, deduce f(6)=6, then by building sequence a_{k+1}=a_k(a_k−1) and monotonicity conclude f(n)=n for all n.
